summary: This informational document proposes guidelines for considering human rights in protocol design, similar to the privacy considerations in RFC 6973. It explains the background and how the guidelines were developed, and is the first milestone of a longer research effort.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet protocols shape how people communicate, find information, and gather. This RFC asks protocol authors to consider and document how their design choices may affect human rights.

subtitle: A research framework for considering how protocol choices can affect people's rights.

tldr.problem: Protocol design choices can support or restrict human rights, but engineers need a way to examine those effects openly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents research, a shared vocabulary, examples of technical concepts and rights, and questions for protocol authors to consider.
tldr.outcome: It is an initial Informational research document and has been updated by RFC 9620.

today: RFC 8280 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 9620. It describes itself as an early milestone in a longer research effort, not as an Internet Standards Track specification.

sections.title: Why Protocol Design Matters
sections.content:
The Internet can enable rights such as freedom of expression and association, but design choices can also restrict them. Rights may conflict, so a protocol's effects should be made clear enough for people to discuss and balance them.

The RFC aims to connect technical design with human rights, propose considerations for future Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) protocol work, and raise awareness in both technical and human-rights communities. It does not claim that technology alone can guarantee rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet design can affect people's ability to speak and gather. Authors should make those effects visible, including when different rights may conflict.

sections.title: Research Questions and Method
sections.content:
The research group asked how protocols can enable or restrict human rights, and whether guidelines could improve informed and transparent decisions. Its method combined analysis of RFCs and mailing lists with interviews and observation of working groups.

The researchers used automated analysis to identify technical concepts, then reviewed the material qualitatively because word counts cannot explain meaning by themselves. They built a shared vocabulary to support discussion across technical and human-rights fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers studied Internet standards and discussions, interviewed community members, and observed working groups. They combined computer-assisted searches with human interpretation.

sections.title: Technical Concepts and Rights
sections.content:
The RFC relates concepts such as connectivity, privacy, security, content agnosticism, internationalization, censorship resistance, open standards, and accessibility to rights. It also discusses concepts such as anonymity, pseudonymity, decentralization, reliability, confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity.

These relationships are an initial mapping, not a complete or exhaustive account. The RFC uses examples to show that a technical feature can support one interest while creating risks in a different context.
sections.plainLanguage: Features such as privacy, secure communication, and broad access can help people exercise their rights. The RFC's examples show possible effects, not a final judgment about a protocol.

sections.title: Questions for Protocol Authors
sections.content:
The proposed considerations give protocol authors questions about how their design affects people and systems. They cover technical qualities that may shape access, privacy, security, censorship, and other rights-related outcomes.

The questions are not a checklist of required technical solutions. The RFC says the range of protocols is too broad for one set of practices; the purpose is to support a documented discussion and encourage consideration of alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors can use the questions to discuss who might gain or lose access, privacy, or security. The questions prompt analysis; they do not prescribe one design for every protocol.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it introduces no security considerations because it presents research rather than a protocol. It also requires no IANA actions.

The document's role is to provide a framework for discussion. It does not define new protocol behavior or technical requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC presents research and questions, not a new protocol. It therefore creates no IANA work and defines no new security mechanism.
